newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge refuses to acquit boxing promoter King.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge refuses to acquit boxing promoter King.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent
Boxing promoter Don King on Monday lost a round in his efforts to halt a new trial on insurance-fraud charges when a federal judge refused to acquit him after a 1995 mistrial in the case.
A spokesman for the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office said prosecutors will proceed and seek a new trial date.

King, one of the world's leading boxing promoters, was tried on nine counts of insurance fraud involving a 1991 Julio Cesar Chavez fight that was cancelled. Each count carried a maximum five-year prison sentence and a $250,000 fine.

He was accused of padding his claim submitted to Lloyd's of London with $350,000 in training-fee losses that did not occur. The insurance contract covered non-refundable expenses and Lloyd's paid King a total of $671,000.

In denying King's motion for acquittal, U.S. District Judge Lawrence McKenna said as a matter of law he had "taken as true" all testimony from government witnesses, but he did not consider the credibility of the witnesses or the weight of the evidence.

"The court's conclusion is based on what a rational juror could find as fact and what inferences favourable to the government a rational juror could draw from facts found, and does not represent findings of fact by the court or inferences drawn by the court."

Although witnesses testified during the trial that King kept tight control over his company, insisting on signing checks for as little as five cents, the promoter testified he had nothing to do with the filing of the Lloyd's claim.

Chavez, who was scheduled to fight Harold Brazier in 1991 in Las Vegas, was injured before the fight and it was cancelled. Prosecutors alleged King never told Chavez about the $350,000 insurance claim and illegally pocketed the money.

The trial, which started on Sept. 21, 1995, ended on Nov. 17 when McKenna took the unusual step of declaring a mistrial after the jury first told him it could not reach a verdict. Normally a judge instructs a panel to go back and keep trying.

The judge said the jury was "irretrievably deadlocked" and it would be unfair to pressure them to reach a decision because one panellist could not remain past the next day. It was left unclear why the deliberations could not continue with 11 jurors or an alternate.

King has been a defendant several times before and served four years in prison after being convicted in 1967 of beating a man to death in Cleveland. He was also accused of killing a man in 1954 but never stood trial as he was found to have acted in self-defence.
He was acquitted of federal tax-evasion charges in 1985.
